intent: Construct a field, oscillator or circuit model with a stated system boundary; predict its spatial or temporal behavior; connect the prediction to energy and charge conservation; and test the model against independently computed or explicitly synthetic evidence.
courseObjectives: Reconstruct oscillatory motion from initial conditions, distinguish free and driven responses, and assess damping and resonance within a stated model.
Relate wave functions, boundary conditions, energy transport and measurements while distinguishing a moving pattern from motion of the medium.
Calculate electric and magnetic fields from specified sources and identify when symmetry makes an integral law a usable solution method.
Relate electric potential, work, capacitance, polarization and stored energy with consistent reference choices and source conditions.
Predict DC transients and AC response, including real instrument loading, using signed conservation equations and dimensionally valid component laws.
Connect induction and electromagnetic waves to Maxwell's equations, charge continuity, field energy and power flow.
Evaluate uncertainty, numerical convergence and competing models; preserve reproducible evidence and explain limitations without claiming a physical experiment occurred.
sequenceRationale: Begin with the time-domain oscillator that students can connect to mechanics. Use waves to establish phase, superposition and boundary conditions. Develop sources, fields and energy before circuit approximations, then magnetic interactions and induction before AC power and Maxwell's synthesis. A final numerical check and sustained investigation require evidence across these representations. This is our proposed self-study sequence.

conventions.units: Use SI and supply requested units on inputs, axes, coefficients, solutions and interpretations. Angular arguments are radians; distinguish angular frequency in rad/s from cyclic frequency in Hz. C, F, H, T, Wb, V and ohm are introduced with mechanical dimensions.
conventions.signs: Define coordinate axes, normals, loop orientation, charge sign and current reference before calculating. Use outward normals for closed surfaces and a right-hand relation between a chosen loop and its area vector. State passive sign convention for absorbed circuit power. Electron drift and conventional current may oppose each other.
conventions.phase: Use x(t)=A cos(omega t+phi) and real-part phasors with exp(j omega t) unless explicitly stated otherwise. A is nonnegative. Distinguish equivalent phases modulo 2 pi from a requested principal interval, and state whether phasors are peak or RMS. Define the zero-amplitude phase as indeterminate rather than silently choosing a physical phase.
conventions.fields: Separate source and observation coordinates. State integration measure and density units, excluded singular points, material region and boundary assumptions. Zero enclosed charge establishes zero net flux, not necessarily zero field. Electrostatic potential cannot globally describe an induced electric field with nonzero circulation.
conventions.constants: Use stated rounded constants consistently and test derived relations. The NIST 2022 CODATA table supplies references: c=299792458 m/s and elementary charge=1.602176634e-19 C are exact definitions; vacuum permittivity and permeability are measured constants, not exact 4 pi conventions. Each generated form prints the constants used; learners need not memorize them.
conventions.approximation: Make linearity, small amplitude, lumped-element, quasi-static, ideal conductor, uniform medium, nonrelativistic motion and lossless assumptions explicit where used. Check operating domains and limiting cases instead of treating every formula as universal.
conventions.precision: Preserve internal precision. Exact rational, radical or pi fields accept supported equivalents; approximate fields state tolerance and units. Include numerical methods and domain restrictions in solutions. Display rounding must not change a critical boundary decision.
